title: The Letters of the Crescent Cove
premise: Beatrix Eastwick, a cellist who walked off stage mid-concert five years ago after a panic attack she never explained, has built a quiet life in Crescent Cove teaching music and avoiding anything that might break her again. When Elias Thorne—the stranger who has written her anonymous letters of encouragement for a decade—moves in next door to restore his late grandmother's house before selling it, Beatrix realizes the letters were never anonymous at all: he is the boy from the summer music camp who heard her play once and never forgot. As they restore the house together and fall in love, Beatrix discovers the sale will erase the boathouse where they first met, forcing her to choose between protecting her safe life and fighting publicly for something worth being seen for. In the end, Beatrix performs again—at a benefit concert that saves the boathouse—and chooses Elias, learning that love means letting someone stay even when every instinct says to run.
about_author: Astrid Dunmore is the pen name of a former orchestral librarian who spent fifteen years touring with chamber ensembles before turning to fiction full-time. She writes love stories set in coastal towns, drawn to characters who must choose between the lives they've carefully built and the ones that terrify them.

chapters.title: The Last Train
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Five years after walking off stage at Wigmore Hall, Beatrix teaches cello in sleepy Crescent Cove, her days measured in small safe routines. A moving van arrives next door at the derelict Harrow house. She watches from behind her curtain, telling herself new neighbors mean nothing. Emotional beat: the fragile peace of a life built on avoidance.

chapters.title: Letters I Never Sent Back
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Unpacking boxes, Beatrix rereads a decade of unsigned letters that arrived after her collapse—letters that somehow knew exactly what she needed to hear. The newest one mentions Crescent Cove. Her hands shake. Emotional beat: the letters are her most private comfort, and someone may be closer than she ever imagined.

chapters.title: The Man with the Blue Tarp
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias Thorne moves into his late grandmother's house intending a quick renovation and sale—a tidy way to close the past. He recognizes his neighbor instantly as the cellist from music camp whose playing changed his life. He says nothing. Emotional beat: hope tangled with guilt over a deception ten years deep.

chapters.title: Borrowed Sugar, Borrowed Time
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Forced proximity: a storm knocks out power and Elias appears at her door with candles and an old generator. Their first real conversation is easy, disarming, dangerous. She notices he watches her hands when she mentions the cello. Emotional beat: the first crack in her armor, terrifyingly pleasant.

chapters.title: What the Boathouse Remembers
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Elias discovers his grandmother's will requires the boathouse on the property be preserved or the whole estate passes to a conservation trust he can't afford to fight. Beatrix finds him staring at the rotting structure; it's where she played the summer he first heard her. Neither says so. Emotional beat: two secrets circling the same memory.

chapters.title: Duet, Unrehearsed
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Beatrix catches Elias humming the exact piece she performed at camp. Cornered by coincidence, he admits hearing her play once, long ago—but not the letters. They play together, her first time performing for anyone in five years, just the two of them in the half-gutted parlor. Emotional beat: joy that feels like trespassing.

chapters.title: The Student Who Wouldn't Quit
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Her boldest student, twelve-year-old Priya, demands to enter the regional youth concerto competition and asks Beatrix to coach her publicly. Saying yes means standing on a stage again, even at the edge of one. Elias encourages her; she snaps at him. Emotional beat: duty to others versus fear for herself.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Letters
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Renovating the attic, Elias finds his grandmother's correspondence—including drafts of letters in his own handwriting she'd encouraged, and her note: 'Tell her someday, or the house will tell her for you.' He burns nothing but can't throw anything away either. Emotional beat: inheritance as obligation, not just property.

chapters.title: Low Tide, High Stakes
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. A developer's surveyor measures the boathouse; word spreads the Harrow estate will be sold to a hotel chain. Beatrix realizes losing the boathouse means losing the last physical place her old self existed. She starts a petition almost without deciding to—her first public act in years. Emotional beat: grief converting, slowly, into fight.

chapters.title: Almost Confessions
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. A festival night on the beach; wine, lanterns, almost-kiss interrupted by Elias's phone call from the buyer's lawyer. Later, alone, Beatrix tells Elias about the concert she fled—everything except why. He nearly tells her about the letters. Both retreat. Emotional beat: intimacy outpacing honesty, which cannot last.

chapters.title: Priya's Audition
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Beatrix coaches Priya through her audition, hiding backstage in terror while her student plays brilliantly. Watching someone else be brave on stage undoes her. Elias finds her crying in the corridor and holds her; this time she lets him. Emotional beat: borrowed courage is still courage.

chapters.title: The Buyer Arrives
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. The hotel developer's representative visits; the offer would solve Elias's debts and honor nothing. His grandmother's trust clause gives him ninety days to raise matching funds or prove community value. Beatrix organizes a benefit concert proposal—with herself named as performer. He sees what it costs her to volunteer. Emotional beat: love against duty, both directions.

chapters.title: Rehearsal in Ruins
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. First rehearsal in the crumbling boathouse itself, strings detuning in the sea air, half the town watching. Beatrix's hands seize mid-phrase—an echo of the panic attack. Elias quietly stops the room and sits beside her until she breathes again. Emotional beat: public failure survived, barely, together.

chapters.title: Why I Walked Off Stage
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Beatrix finally tells Elias the truth: her mentor and lover had died suddenly weeks before the Wigmore concert, and the piece was one they'd planned to premiere together. Playing it felt like drowning. Elias listens without fixing. Emotional beat: the deepest lock opened; grief given somewhere to go.

chapters.title: The Letter He Wrote First
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias confesses everything: the camp, the decade of letters, his grandmother's role in encouraging them. Beatrix's reaction is not gratitude—it's betrayal. 'You knew me for ten years and let me think I was alone.' She walks out into the rain. Emotional beat: the truth arriving too late to feel like a gift.

chapters.title: Silence Between Movements
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Two weeks of silence. Beatrix throws herself into Priya's coaching and the benefit logistics, hollowed out. She rereads the letters and realizes every one of them told the truth about her—even if the signature lied. Elias leaves the house keys in her mailbox and a single line: 'The boathouse was never mine to sell.' Emotional beat: anger cooling into reckoning.

chapters.title: The Trust Clause
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Deadline week. Elias refuses the developer's final offer, gambling the entire estate on the benefit concert raising enough to endow the boathouse as a community music school. He signs papers making Beatrix artistic director regardless of whether she forgives him. Emotional beat: duty finally aligned with love instead of against it.

chapters.title: Tuning in the Dark
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Night before the concert, Beatrix finds Elias asleep in the boathouse among folding chairs, exhausted, having worked three days straight. She wakes him; they talk honestly about fear, forgiveness, and what staying actually means. No promises yet—just presence. Emotional beat: reconciliation not as erasure but as choice.

chapters.title: The Benefit Concert
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The concert: full town, storm-threatened sky, Priya opening. Beatrix takes the stage last, plays the piece she fled five years ago, and finishes it—hands steady, tears falling, Elias in the front row. The donations counter climbs past the endowment threshold as she bows. Emotional beat: climax; the catastrophic performance answered at last.

chapters.title: What the House Decided
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. The trust is funded; the developer withdraws. Elias learns his grandmother's will contained one more letter, held by her solicitor, to be delivered only if the boathouse survived—her blessing, written years ago, addressed to 'the girl who plays.' Beatrix reads it and weeps. Emotional beat: inheritance revealed as love arranged in advance.

chapters.title: After the Last Train Leaves
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Weeks later: the boathouse school opens, Priya wins her competition, and Beatrix accepts a small local recital series—not a comeback, a continuation. On the platform, seeing Elias onto a train to settle his affairs elsewhere, she realizes she doesn't want the platform to empty. Emotional beat: the moment avoidance dies.

chapters.title: Someone Who Stays
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Elias returns early, unannounced, having leased the cottage rather than sold the house. Beatrix meets him at the gate with two mugs and no speech. Final scene: the two of them playing duets in the restored boathouse as students arrive below, the letters framed on the wall, signed at last. Emotional beat: resolution—love chosen openly, memory honored, home redefined.
